item.question: The source's Attention principle asks for two distinct things. What are they, and what means does it name for achieving them?
item.answer: Hooking attention and sustaining it — "Hook and sustain attention with an immersive story" — so an arresting opening that then loses the viewer does not satisfy the principle. The means named for both is audio and visuals together: "Drop viewers in from the start and immerse them with audio and visuals that pique their interest." The audio half is the one part of Attention for which the source gives a mechanism: music, voice-over and sound effects are said to create a rich, sensory experience that helps people pay attention. What it never gives is a duration — no page names a number of seconds for "the start".
item.support: The principle statement is in the core table; the immersion instruction and the audio mechanism are on the resources article and Think with Google respectively.

item.question: The source states that "YouTube is almost entirely a sound-on experience". What is the scope of that claim, and what would it be wrong to conclude from it?
item.answer: It is a claim about how one named platform was being watched, made once, on the Think with Google page dated April 2022, and offered as the reason to exploit the multisensory nature of the medium. It is not a claim about short-form or feed video in general, and it points the opposite way from the sound-off default that other feed surfaces are usually designed against. No measurement, figure or study is attached to it. Neither of the other two pages states it, even though guidelines on both — reinforcing branding with audio, supercharging the CTA with voice-over, supporting the story with audio — depend on it being true. Viewing behaviour changes, so a claim of this kind is true of a period, and the source names no period beyond its own date.

item.question: A performance team wants to put the call to action in the first two seconds of an action-objective ad, to catch viewers who skip. What does this source's own guidance say about that placement?
item.answer: It says the opposite, and it is the source's only placement instruction anywhere. The action row's Direction cell reads "Present the ask after the context is set", and the objective's own statement is "Present an enticing call-to-action with the right context" — so on this source's account the context precedes the ask for exactly this objective. Two qualifications belong in the answer. The core Direction guidance says nothing about placement at all, so there is no general end-of-ad rule here to appeal to either. And the full-funnel row goes a third way — "Use CTAs throughout your ad, and be more direct as you go" — but that is a different objective, and it does not license a front-loaded ask on an action brief.
item.support: The action row's Direction cell and the objective's own description both order context before the ask; the core Direction row contains no placement guidance.

source_terms: The most effective testimonial commercials are those which show loyal users of your product testifying to its virtues – when they don't know they are being filmed.
The interviewer pretends to find fault with the product and the loyal user rises to its defense with far more conviction than if you simply asked him what he thought of it.
The more amateurish the performance, the more credible.
item.claim: The most effective testimonial commercials show loyal users testifying when they do not know they are being filmed, and the source describes a specific device for producing conviction: the interviewer attacks the product and the user rises to its defence, which he says produces far more conviction than asking what the user thinks. He states the selection rule that follows — avoid users who would give so polished a performance that viewers would take them for professional actors, because the more amateurish the performance the more credible it is. His supporting case is a French campaign that cast an eighty-year-old laundress as its heroine; she became recognised by three in four people in France and the product is reported to have moved from fourth to second in sales.

mechanism.text: Credibility comes from the speaker appearing not to be performing for the advertiser. Defending the product against an attack, and doing it clumsily, are both signals that the speech is the speaker's own.

caveats.text: the mechanism is a claim about how sincerity is read, and the technique described — filming people who do not know they are being filmed, with an actor posing as a dealer — is a staged authenticity, which the source does not comment on
the French washing-machine case reports a recognition figure and a sales rank change with no other cause excluded; recognition is measured, the rank change is attributed
this claim and the celebrity finding are the same underlying argument about perceived interest, stated from the two ends

source_stated_remedies: let the interviewer attack the product so the user defends it
avoid users whose performance would look professional

positive.description: a hidden-camera Shell forecourt commercial in which an actor posing as the dealer disparages the fuel and a customer defends it, reproduced in the book as a script

intra_source_relations.note: the television form of the testimonial credibility claim

source_terms: The Law of Credentials
The crucial ingredient in the success of any brand is its claim to authenticity.
Credentials are the collateral you put up to guarantee the performance of your brand.
item.claim: Law 6. The authors start from customer disbelief: prospects are suspicious and discount most product claims. They argue one claim takes precedence over all others because it makes the others credible — the claim to authenticity, to being the real thing. Benefit claims made without credentials are, on their account, generally ignored, because every competitor makes the same sort of claim; the same benefit claims attached to a credential carry much more weight. They extend the point to buyer behaviour generally with the empty-restaurant observation: people prefer to wait for a table where there is a queue rather than eat in an empty room.

mechanism.text: Credentials work as collateral. A claim about performance is unverifiable at the point of choice, so the prospect looks for something that stands behind it; where a brand supplies that, the prospect will believe almost anything else it says. Absent it, benefit claims fall into the undifferentiated mass that provokes "that's what they all say".

scope.conditions: wherever prospects cannot verify a product claim before buying

caveats.text: 'the crucial ingredient in the success of any brand' is a universal claim demonstrated by one advertising line (Coca-Cola's 'the real thing') and two consulting cases of the authors' own
the Act and Datastream cases are the authors' own client work, reported by them with the outcome figures they chose to report and no independent source

source_stated_problems: many companies run branding programs almost devoid of credentials
an endless parade of almost meaningless benefits . . . they each lack credibility so they are generally ignored
source_stated_remedies: when the benefits are structured around some aspect of a brand's credentials, they carry much more weight

positive.description: Act positioned as 'the largest-selling contact software', with the credential carried on every surface including the box

intra_source_relations.note: leadership is the credential the authors reach for first
credentials are what makes a brand usable to reporters

source_terms: If you include a testimonial in your copy, you make it more credible. Readers find the endorsements of fellow consumers more persuasive than the puffery of anonymous copywriters.
Testimonials from celebrities get high recall scores, but I have stopped using them because readers remember the celebrity and forget the product.
On the other hand, testimonials from experts can be persuasive
item.claim: Testimonials make copy more credible because readers find the endorsement of a fellow consumer more persuasive than the puffery of an anonymous copywriter, and an entire advertisement can be cast as one. Celebrity testimonials, however, score high on recall while the reader remembers the celebrity and forgets the product, and assumes the celebrity was bought — which the source says is usually the case. Expert testimony is exempted: he instances an ex-burglar testifying that he could never crack a particular safe.

mechanism.text: Credibility comes from the endorser being disinterested, so a celebrity known to be paid loses the property that makes a testimonial work, while an expert's standing is not for sale in the same way. Separately, a famous face is a more memorable object than the product beside it.

caveats.text: the celebrity finding is stated in three chapters with three different framings — print recall, television brand preference, and direct response, where the exception is named as recognised authorities such as a golfer endorsing golf clubs. The exception is the same one each time: relevant expertise
the source's own worst-remembered example is his own: paying Eleanor Roosevelt thirty-five thousand dollars for a margarine commercial, which he calls not one of his proudest memories

source_terms: any light positioned within the family of angles will produce a direct reflection
any light positioned outside of the family of angles will not light a mirror-like subject at all, at least as far as the camera can see
item.claim: Whether a direct reflection appears is decided entirely by whether the light sits inside the family of angles. A light inside it produces one; a light outside it does not light a mirror-like subject at all as far as the camera is concerned. To see direct reflection across most of a mirror-like surface, the source must be large enough to fill the family; to see none, both camera and light must be placed so the source falls outside it.

caveats.text: the source states it will use this principle repeatedly in later chapters, marking it as the chapter's operative result
the placement rule is a two-sided control — it says how to obtain the reflection and how to eliminate it — which is unusual among the craft rules seen in this batch

source_stated_remedies: use a light large enough to fill the family of angles to produce direct reflection across the surface
place both camera and light so the source falls outside the family of angles to eliminate direct reflection

source_terms: The family of angles causing direct reflection has grown much larger, and the range of acceptable angles for copy lighting is much smaller.
The same lighting angle that works well when the camera is farther away can cause direct reflection if the camera is closer.
item.claim: Moving the camera closer to a flat subject, with a correspondingly wider lens to keep the framing, enlarges the family of angles that produces direct reflection and shrinks the range of lighting angles that avoid it. Moving the camera farther away with a longer lens does the reverse: the family shrinks and a good lighting angle becomes easy to find. The consequence is that a lighting angle is not portable between set-ups — the same angle that was safe from a distance can produce direct reflection from close in. When the room will not allow the lights to move, the problem can sometimes be solved by moving the camera instead.

mechanism.text: The family of angles is the set of angles over all points of the surface at which a source can reflect to the camera; a closer viewpoint subtends a wider spread of those angles, so the family widens with proximity and narrows with distance.

scope.conditions: flat subjects; the source's cases are a copy stand, a museum wall with a 90-degree horizontal angle of view, and a long-lens set-up

caveats.text: extends the live family-of-angles concept (sk_lsm_c003_0013) from a fixed geometry to a variable the photographer controls; chapter 3 defines the family, this chapter makes its SIZE the operative control
supported by three lighting diagrams rather than photographs; the diagrams were not opened, so the geometry rests on the prose, which states it explicitly

source_terms: Direct reflections are a mirror image of the light source that produces them.

item.claim: A direct reflection is a mirror image of the light source. Light rays bounce from a smooth surface at the same angle at which they strike it, so the point from which a direct reflection can be seen is exactly determined by the angles between source, subject and camera.

source_terms: It shows how applying a good technique at the wrong time can produce a bad picture.
black subjects, by definition, produce little diffuse reflection
item.claim: The raking light that revealed the sponge's texture loses almost all detail in a black leather notebook cover. The shadow side of each texture particle is still there; what has gone is the diffuse highlight on the other side, because a black subject by definition produces little diffuse reflection. The source is explicit that the failure is caused by the subject, not by the technique, and that it will not accept an exposure increase as the answer, both because most scenes also contain light-toned areas whose highlight detail would be lost and because it holds itself to solving lighting problems by lighting.

mechanism.text: Texture is read as a tonal difference between two faces of a particle. Raking light produces that difference by adding a shadow to one face and relying on diffuse reflection for the other. On a black surface the diffuse channel is nearly empty, so only the shadow survives and there is no difference to read.

scope.conditions: dark subjects with surface texture; the source's example is a black leather book cover

caveats.text: the source refuses exposure compensation as a remedy on two stated grounds, one technical and one self-imposed: important light-toned areas exist in most scenes, and the book is about lighting
the pair 4.17 / 4.19 is a genuine matched comparison — the source states the amount of light falling on the leather is the same in both, so the improvement cannot be an exposure effect

source_stated_problems: The lighting that revealed the texture so well in the sponge loses almost all detail in the notebook's cover.

counter.description: black leather notebook under the sponge's raking light: a near-black slab, the embossed pattern invisible

intra_source_relations.note: same technique, opposite result, because the surface differs
the remedy is to switch reflection type

source_terms: The solution is to position the light at a very shallow angle to the surface so that it skims across it
This gives each particle of texture—it gives them, in other words—both a highlight side and a shadow side.
small light sources produce sharply defined shadows
item.claim: A light-toned, strongly diffuse subject photographed with the light on the camera shows almost no texture, because the brightness of a diffuse reflection does not depend on the angle of illumination: light striking the side of a texture particle returns to the camera almost as brightly as light striking its top. The remedy is a very shallow, skimming light that gives each particle a highlight side and a shadow side. The source adds that the source should be as small as possible, because small sources produce sharply defined shadows, and a sharp shadow is more likely to survive the optical limits of resolving very small texture. The uneven illumination this shallow angle causes is cured the same way as in copy work: move the light farther away.

mechanism.text: Texture is read from the tonal difference between the lit and unlit faces of each particle. Diffuse reflection is angle-independent, so frontal light gives both faces the same brightness and the difference vanishes; a grazing angle restores it by shadowing one face.

scope.conditions: medium- and light-toned subjects that reflect mostly diffusely; the source's example is a light-blue sponge

caveats.text: applies the live chapter-3 angle-independence of diffuse reflection (sk_lsm_c003_0004) rather than restating it: this is the practical consequence, that a diffuse subject front-lit has no texture to show
the source says this technique is so easy to understand it is almost intuitive and that novices learn it unaided; it introduces it only to set up the case where the same technique fails

source_stated_problems: With no contrasting highlights and shadows, much of the sponge's surface detail is invisible.
source_stated_remedies: position the light at a very shallow angle so that it skims across the surface
use as small a light source as possible so the texture shadows are sharply defined

positive.description: the same sponge under raking light: the pore structure is fully modelled, every cell carrying a lit edge and a shadowed one

counter.description: a light-blue sponge photographed with a strobe on the camera: an almost featureless blue rectangle

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', sections 'Using Diffuse Reflection and Shadow to Reveal Texture' and 'Capitalizing on Direct Reflections'
item.question: A raking light reveals the texture of a light-blue sponge beautifully and destroys the texture of a black leather notebook. Explain the mechanism, and give the book's remedy for the leather.
item.answer: Texture is read as a tonal difference between two faces of each texture particle. Raking light creates that difference by shadowing one face and relying on diffuse reflection to light the other. The sponge is light-toned and strongly diffuse, so both halves are present. The leather is black, and a black subject by definition produces little diffuse reflection, so the shadow side survives and the diffuse highlight side does not — there is no difference left to read. The authors are explicit that the failure is caused by the subject, not by the technique. Their remedy is to switch the surface to the reflection channel it actually has: a large source above the subject, big enough to fill the whole family of angles, so the leather is rendered by direct reflection instead. They note this is the exact opposite arrangement on both variables — direction and size — and say the earlier theory taken alone would call it the worst possible way to light the leather. The texture highlight moves from near black to middle grey with the same light falling on the subject and no exposure increase.
item.support: Ch. 4, the sponge sequence and then 'Capitalizing on Direct Reflections'. The source states that the amount of light falling on the leather is the same in both leather frames, which is what rules out an exposure explanation.
confounders: answering 'increase the exposure', which the source explicitly refuses on two stated grounds
assuming the leather needs an even harder or more raking light — more of the failing treatment
attributing the difference to colour rather than to the diffuse-reflection channel that colour implies

item.rationale: SPEC-01's visual_language field records lighting among palette, texture and genre. This source supplies what a lighting specification must actually decide: which reflection type is to dominate on which surfaces. The source states that deciding which reflection matters and then capitalising on it is the whole method, and that the choice is the photographer's creative decision rather than one the physics makes.

applicability.when: specifying lighting intent for a still or frame containing surfaces of differing finish
applicability.limits: The source is explicit that the physics constrains without determining; the appropriate choice is a creative decision. This binding therefore supplies vocabulary for expressing an intent, not a rule for choosing one.

source_terms: If we cannot get significant diffuse reflection from the leather surface, we will try to produce direct reflection instead.
the theory that predicts the best way to light the sponge also says that our new lighting arrangement is the worst possible way to light the leather!
The apparent increase in illumination comes from good reflection management.
item.claim: When a surface cannot supply enough diffuse reflection to show its texture, the remedy is to produce direct reflection instead. For the black leather this means a large source, above the subject rather than raking from the side, big enough to fill the whole family of angles. That is the exact opposite of the arrangement that worked for the sponge on every variable — direction and size both inverted — and the source says plainly that the earlier theory, taken alone, predicts this is the worst possible way to light the leather. The apparent contradiction is resolved by the fact that the earlier reasoning considered only diffuse reflection. With the large overhead source the leather's texture highlight moves from near black to middle grey with no exposure increase and the same amount of light falling on the subject.

mechanism.text: The leather produces little diffuse reflection but a great deal of direct reflection. Direct reflection is available only from inside the family of angles, so a source large enough to fill that family lights the whole surface through the channel the surface actually has, raising the recorded highlight without changing the incident light or the exposure.

scope.conditions: dark subjects with a glossy or semi-glossy texture

caveats.text: this is the chapter's own demonstration that a lighting rule cannot be applied without first classifying the surface; the two results are not a contradiction in the physics but a demonstration that the earlier rule had an unstated precondition

builds on the live chapter-3 result that a source filling the family produces direct reflection across a surface (sk_lsm_c003_0014) and on the live explanation that dark subjects show direct reflection more readily because their diffuse reflection is weak (sk_lsm_c003_0017); neither is re-extracted

source_stated_problems: the diffuse highlight on the other side of each particle is gone
source_stated_remedies: find the family of angles and use a light large enough to fill it, so the surface is rendered by direct reflection instead

positive.description: the same black leather under a large overhead source filling the family of angles: the embossed diamond pattern and stitching are fully legible against a mid-grey ground

intra_source_relations.note: names the precondition the raking-light rule silently assumed
the two-step method's own worked case
the same move is later generalised to all black-on-black subjects

source_terms: The action must be well lit so that it can be seen all the time; but in close shots the actors' faces should be the lightest spots on the screen.

(1) all lights are on; (2) no light moves; (3) dimmers are correct; (4) there is no voltage drop; (5) actors return to their designated positions (marks) exactly as in rehearsals; (6) one actor does not shade the face of another too extensively; (7) make-up was not damaged
item.claim: Lighting is finished in two passes with a rehearsal between them. The rehearsal is walked with the principals while stand-ins watch, and it exposes what the rough lighting missed — the source gives an example in which the faces went muddy as the actors crossed the set. Individual keylights are then added and balanced with kickers, with the rule that in close shots the faces should be the lightest spots on the screen. During the take seven specific things are checked, including that no light moves, that there is no voltage drop, that actors return exactly to their marks, and that one actor does not shade another's face.

scope.conditions: a shooting day on a lit set

caveats.text: the seven checks are physical-production conditions of the period; five of the seven have no counterpart outside a stage with electricians and actors

source_stated_problems: the general light was inadequate; the faces were underlit and consequently went muddy
source_stated_remedies: add individual keylights and balance them with kickers

intra_source_relations.note: follows the rough-in

source_terms: The family of angles causing direct reflection has grown much larger, and the range of acceptable angles for copy lighting is much smaller.
The same lighting angle that works well when the camera is farther away can cause direct reflection if the camera is closer.
item.claim: Moving the camera closer to a flat subject, with a correspondingly wider lens to keep the framing, enlarges the family of angles that produces direct reflection and shrinks the range of lighting angles that avoid it. Moving the camera farther away with a longer lens does the reverse: the family shrinks and a good lighting angle becomes easy to find. The consequence is that a lighting angle is not portable between set-ups — the same angle that was safe from a distance can produce direct reflection from close in. When the room will not allow the lights to move, the problem can sometimes be solved by moving the camera instead.

mechanism.text: The family of angles is the set of angles over all points of the surface at which a source can reflect to the camera; a closer viewpoint subtends a wider spread of those angles, so the family widens with proximity and narrows with distance.

scope.conditions: flat subjects; the source's cases are a copy stand, a museum wall with a 90-degree horizontal angle of view, and a long-lens set-up

caveats.text: extends the live family-of-angles concept (sk_lsm_c003_0013) from a fixed geometry to a variable the photographer controls; chapter 3 defines the family, this chapter makes its SIZE the operative control
supported by three lighting diagrams rather than photographs; the diagrams were not opened, so the geometry rests on the prose, which states it explicitly

source_stated_problems: the room may make the placement of the lights more difficult than that of the camera
source_stated_remedies: move the camera farther away from the subject and use a correspondingly longer lens to shrink the family of angles
move the light farther to the side when a close viewpoint has enlarged the family

intra_source_relations.note: there is no fixed safe lighting angle; it depends on viewpoint
the same control reappears as the effective size of the light on metal
moving the camera to control the family also changes perspective distortion
